title: Teresa of Kolkata (1910–1997)
hookLine: a teacher leaves her convent to care for the dying poor, and writes later of long spiritual darkness
tomorrow: Camp 2 close: the cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1)

cards: September 1946. A nun in her thirties is on a crowded overnight train from Calcutta up into the hills of Darjeeling, heading for a retreat.
For nearly twenty years she's taught geography and history to girls at a convent school, behind walls, in a city full of people sleeping and dying on the pavements outside.
Somewhere on that train, she said later, she heard a call inside her call: leave the convent, and go to live with the poorest of the poor.
She was born in Skopje as Anjezë Bojaxhiu, and as a nun she took her name from a saint you met two days ago, Thérèse of Lisieux.

teach.h: A WHITE SARI, INTO THE SLUMS.
teach.b: It took her two years to get permission. In 1948 she put on a cheap white sari with blue borders, took some basic nursing training, and walked into the slums with almost nothing. A few of her former students joined her.
In 1950 the Church approved her new order, the Missionaries of Charity.
Soon after, she opened a home for the dying in an old building beside the Kali temple in Kalighat, where people found in the street could die washed, fed, and held, whatever their religion.
She called it Nirmal Hriday, pure heart. The order spread to cities all over the world, and in 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize. Here's what few people knew until after she died in 1997.
Her letters, published in 2007, showed that for close to fifty years, from around the time she started this work, she felt God's absence.
She wrote of darkness and emptiness, and that she no longer felt the presence she'd felt on that train. She kept going anyway, every day, on the floor with the sick.
She had critics too, over the medical care in her homes and some of her funding, and people still argue about that. In 2016 Pope Francis declared her a saint.
Her way was close to her namesake's: she is often quoted as saying most of us can't do great things, only small things with great love.
Catholics see in her the words of Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

how: Catholics keep the feast of St. Teresa of Calcutta on September 5, the day she died; the Missionaries of Charity continue her work in homes for the dying, the sick and the abandoned around the world, and volunteers often serve alongside them.

games.q: you're a nun who has taught at a convent school for nearly twenty years. on a train you sense a call to leave and live with the poorest. what do you do?
o: stay where you are; you're already serving God.
leave right away, without asking anyone.
ask permission, wait, and then go into the slums.
games.why: she asked, and it took two years to get permission. in 1948 she put on a white sari and walked into the slums with almost nothing.

practice: Think of the next person you'll actually be face to face with: a coworker, a cashier, someone at home.

Picture their face and try to see them as she tried to see the dying on the pavement, not a task, not a problem, a person, and notice one thing about them you usually miss. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
